descriptions.ai_verbatim: Pasted the prompt into an AI chatbot and submitted its answer unchanged.
descriptions.ai_round: Asked an AI, then rounded the numbers to multiples of 5 because they looked cleaner.
descriptions.ai_gut: Asked an AI, then moved a few soldiers onto the castle that felt most important.
descriptions.ai_plus1: Asked an AI, then bumped round-number castles by +1 to win ties.
descriptions.meta_level2: Assumed most entries are proportional or AI '+1' answers and computed the exact best response.
descriptions.meta_simulator: Imagined a population of applicants, simulated both games, and best-responded to it.
descriptions.meta_ai_sampler: Asked the AI several times to see what AI users would submit, then best-responded to that.
descriptions.meta_equilibrium: Played a random draw from the Colonel Blotto Nash equilibrium (unexploitable on average).
descriptions.meta_contrarian: Predicted the crowd would fight over castles 4-5 and built around skipping one of them.
descriptions.human_proportional: Split soldiers in proportion to castle points, rounding by hand.
descriptions.human_top_heavy: Ignored the cheap castles and stacked the valuable ones.
descriptions.human_all_in: Bet everything on one or two castles.
descriptions.human_plus1: Guessed what most people do and added one soldier to beat it.
descriptions.human_random: Low effort: typed numbers that roughly added up.
descriptions.human_underdog: Fought for the cheap castles everyone else ignores.

There's no provably optimal Blotto allocation, so I imagined a likely field of submissions (even splits, proportional, 0/10/20/30/40-style, heavy top-end), worked out by hand how candidate allocations scored against it, and did no actual simulation. In Game 1 the scoring is average points, so each castle is a separate contest. Conceding castle 3 while slightly overbidding the common round numbers on castles 2, 4 and 5 scored best and held up well across the fields I tried. In Game 2 you have to beat the maximum of three opponents and placement is what counts, so I picked the cheapest pair of castles that guarantees first place (3+5 = 8 of 15) and gave them enough margin. These numbers rest on my guesses about other players, not on data.
Assumed mostly proportional / AI-style entries and computed the exact best response to that guess.

game2_top10.reasoning: I assumed the field would mostly be AI-style allocations near the proportional 7/13/20/27/33 split, some leaning toward castles 4 and 5, plus a minority going all-in on the top castles, bunched on round and round-plus-one numbers. In Game 1 the average-score rule means each castle is its own contest against the field, so I gave up castle 4 (where the field is high and bunched) and sat just above the common values on the other four, which wins about 11 points against typical opponents and stays reasonable against all-in players. In Game 2 a castle requires beating the highest of three opponents and first place pays far more than the rest, so I aimed for a guaranteed majority (castles 1+2+5 = 8 points) with a very heavy castle 5 and small edges on the castles AI answers tend to neglect. These choices rest on guesses about the field, not certainty, and copies of this same answer would tie each other.
AI (opus) suggested 1/1/23/33/42; I added +1 to round numbers to win ties.

I guessed that a mostly AI-assisted field would use proportional (about 7/13/20/27/33), round-number (0/10/20/30/40) or plus-one variants, with little on castles 1-2 and rarely more than 55 on castle 5. Because Game 1 is scored by average points, each castle can be judged on its own, so I placed soldiers just above the common clusters on castles 3-5 (23/33/42) and put one soldier each on castles 1-2 to turn the many 0-0 ties into wins. For Game 2, where finishing place matters and first is worth 9, I aimed for castles 1+2+5 (8 of 15 points, which guarantees first) because the field neglects the small castles and rarely sends 65 or more to castle 5. This is a bet on the field, not a guaranteed winner; it does poorly against unusual extreme or very even allocations.

For Game 1, I noted that the score is additive average points, so each castle is an independent bet against the field's spread at that castle. I estimated that the field bunches around proportional or slightly top-heavy allocations and round numbers, priced what it costs to beat most of the field at each castle, and dropped castles 1 and 2 as the cheapest points to give up, placing 26/33/41 just above the expected bunches. For Game 2, the four-player format and 1st-place-heavy payout favor concentrating. I expected castle 5 to be over-contested by others who concentrate, so I took castles 3 and 4 with large margins: 7 points usually wins because the other 8 points are split three ways. The numbers are judgment calls about likely opponent behavior, not provably optimal.
Asked the AI 8 times to see what AI users will submit, assumed ~43% non-AI entries, and best-responded to that field.

In Game 1 the score is average points, so each castle can be treated separately. I guessed that the field would mostly submit proportional splits, all 20s, ladders and round numbers, and put soldiers just above those levels on the high-value castles, with small tokens on the cheap ones. In Game 2 the payout heavily rewards first place and each castle needs the highest bid of four players, so concentrating beats spreading out. I chose castles 4+3 over 5+3 or 5+4 because castle 5 is likely to be fought over by players going all in. All of this depends on guesses about what other applicants will submit, so these are well-reasoned bets rather than provably optimal answers.
